channel.title: Petr Fedin — feed
channel.description: Fashion-industry analysis and news from my products.

item.title: Syntha now runs deals across multiple legal entities
item.description: Syntha now runs deals across multiple legal entities. In fashion wholesale, a brand, a distributor and a production partner almost never operate through one legal entity, especially when foreign counterparties are in the chain.

item.title: In Renova, an enquiry becomes a project in a single step
item.description: In Renova, an enquiry becomes a project in a single step. Until now a renovation lead and a working project were only loosely connected: turning an enquiry into a project with a contractor, a client and a schedule meant checking by hand who was who.

item.title: ChatX now has a company wiki
item.description: ChatX now has a company wiki. Knowledge is usually kept everywhere except the messenger: pinned messages, files on a drive, in the heads of the longest-serving staff.

item.title: Material purchasing now runs inside Syntha
item.description: Material purchasing now runs inside Syntha. Previously, the supplier request, quote, approval and order were handled manually, outside the system that already holds the specification and the collection volume.

item.title: ChatX now suggests what to reply
item.description: ChatX now suggests what to reply. Coming back to a chat after a meeting and working out what happened over two hours takes real effort, and writing a substantive reply rather than “ok, will check” is harder still.

item.title: Renova stops losing actions when the connection drops
item.description: Renova no longer loses actions when the connection drops. On a site or on the road, connectivity fails regularly. If the app was sending an action at that moment – sign off a stage, confirm a payment – it must neither be lost nor run twice.

item.title: Stores count in days, brands in seasons
item.description: The data behind collection decisions arrives later than the decisions are due. A season runs three to six months, and the summary of it is put together at the end.

item.title: Inditex: revenue up 8.4%, ahead of forecasts, but profit misses
item.description: At Inditex (Zara), sales growth and profit growth have parted ways: costs are outrunning revenue. For a brand owner, it is a prompt to check exactly what you are paying for when sales rise.

item.title: Italian fashion exports: −2.3% on average, but from +6.8% in Hong Kong to −9.6% in Japan
item.description: Italian fashion revenue in 2026 is expected at €91.4bn. That is 1.6% below last year but well ahead of the first forecast. The story is not the total but the spread between countries.

item.title: A Vietnamese seamstress costs three times her Bangladeshi peer – and factories are answering with robots
item.description: Vietnam pays a seamstress about $300 a month and is not trying to cut that pay: it is raising output instead. For a buyer, the question shifts from “where is it cheapest?” to “where is it faster and steadier?”

item.title: £3.9bn a year: what UK retail loses on goods never meant for sale
item.description: Drapers has estimated a hidden cost line in British fashion retail. If it is not a separate line in your P&L, you probably do not know your own figure.

item.title: Japan’s online fashion market to grow from $32.4bn to $86.2bn by 2033
item.description: Nearly every adult in Japan already has internet and a smartphone, yet the market is still growing 15.2% a year. For a brand eyeing Japan, the question is not whether shoppers can reach your site but how you plug into local channels.

item.title: From 19 July 2026, the EU bans destroying unsold clothing
item.description: An ESPR requirement stops being a plan and becomes law, with an exact date. For a brand selling into the EU, it changes how leftover stock is handled right now.

item.title: 46% of fashion executives expect 2026 to worsen, up from 39% a year ago
item.description: McKinsey and BoF report that pessimism is rising for a third year running. For a brand owner, that means planning without waiting for things to “clear up”.

item.title: 400–500 clothing stores closed in a year as the empty-shelves boost fades
item.description: In 2025, 400–500 clothing stores closed in Russia. For a brand, that marks the end of easy mall space and the start of real bargaining with landlords.

item.title: 92% of fashion companies are raising AI budgets, and only 1% call their projects mature
item.description: Almost the whole industry is putting money into AI, yet hardly anyone has a mature project. For a brand owner, that means the gap to competitors is smaller than their press releases suggest.

item.title: China’s luxury market in 2026: six shifts, and none is about “young and digital”
item.description: Jing Daily names six consumer shifts in Chinese luxury for 2026. Together they break the familiar buyer profile: young, digital, fond of “quiet luxury”.

item.title: What Grazia asked about the future of fashion
item.description: Grazia asked fashion experts what the industry will look like in five years, following the BRICS+ Fashion Summit. I was quoted first among those invited. My answer: the brands that win will be the ones that combine creative instinct with precise calculation.
